tip: चरणस्पर्श (charan-sparsh) is literally 'foot-touch' – a greeting for elders. You can say it without bending down, even on the phone: the word alone carries the respect.
तशरीफ़ रखिए (tashreef rakhiye) is literally 'place your honor' – ultra-courteous Urdu-flavored 'please sit'. The guest's honor takes the seat, not the guest.
Hindi has no verb for 'have'. आपके भाई-बहन हैं (aapke bhai-behen hain) is literally 'your brothers-sisters are?' – what you 'have' simply exists as yours.
खाना खाया आपने? (khana khaya aapne = did you eat?) works as a warm hello, like 'how are you?' – it signals care, not curiosity about your actual meal.
तू (tu) is the most intimate of Hindi's three words for 'you' – close friends, kids, God. With a stranger it can insult. The safe default is आप (aap).
आना (aana) is just the infinitive 'to come', used here as a soft, friendly request – 'do come over'. It lands gentler than the bare command आ (aa).
भाई (bhai = brother) attaches to any man's name as friendly respect – कमल भाई (Kamal bhai) is not your sibling. Hindi lends family words to everyone.
जी (ji) alone at the start of a reply means 'yes' or 'sure' – the same syllable that adds respect after a name. One tiny word, two polite jobs.
